approach: The authors conduct a narrative review synthesizing existing literature on microbiota-metabolite-immune interactions. They organize the content by metabolite class (SCFAs, bile acids, tryptophan derivatives, others), detailing biosynthesis, signaling targets, and immunoregulatory effects. The review integrates mechanistic insights from preclinical models with clinical observations regarding ICI responsiveness. It concludes by evaluating translational platforms, specifically immune-competent organoid co-cultures, for dissecting these complex interactions.

contribution_and_limits.contribution: Provides a comprehensive classification and mechanistic summary of gut microbiota-derived metabolites in GI cancer immunotherapy, linking specific metabolites to immune cell phenotypes and ICI outcomes.
contribution_and_limits.limits: As a narrative review, it synthesizes findings from diverse studies without performing new primary experiments or systematic meta-analysis. The context-dependency of metabolite effects implies that generalizations may not apply uniformly across all patient subgroups or cancer types.

key_findings.finding: SCFAs enhance CD8+ T-cell activity and barrier integrity but may also promote immune tolerance (Tregs) and resistance to CTLA-4 blockade under specific conditions.

Secondary bile acids (e.g., DCA, LCA) promote tumorigenesis and immunosuppression via ROS, DNA damage, and m6A modification, whereas protective bile acids (UDCA, TUDCA) counteract these effects and enhance anti-PD-1 efficacy.
Tryptophan metabolism yields both immunosuppressive (kynurenine) and protective (indole derivatives) metabolites that regulate T-cell differentiation and barrier function.
Inosine, TMAO, and Urolithin A show potential as immunotherapy sensitizers by enhancing CD8+ T-cell function or mitochondrial fitness, though some (like 4-HPA) drive resistance.

problem_or_question: To address the limited and heterogeneous efficacy of ICIs in GI cancers by identifying novel biomarkers and adjuvant strategies. Specifically, it aims to elucidate how gut microbiota-derived metabolites shape the tumor immune microenvironment and mediate responses to PD-1/PD-L1 and CTLA-4 blockade.
research_scope: Gastrointestinal (GI) cancers, including colorectal, gastric, hepatocellular, and biliary tract malignancies; focuses on the role of gut microbiota-derived metabolites in immune regulation and response to immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs).
work_summary: This review summarizes current insights into how gut microbiota-derived metabolites modulate host immunity and influence the efficacy of immunotherapy in GI cancers. It categorizes major metabolite classes—short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs), bile acids, tryptophan derivatives, and emerging molecules like inosine and TMAO—and details their context-dependent mechanisms involving metabolic reprogramming, epigenetic regulation, and immune cell modulation. The paper also discusses clinical prospects, including dietary interventions, probiotics, and engineered microbes, while highlighting immune-competent organoid co-culture systems as tools for pre-evaluating these strategies.
